lessons.title: Everyone Is Already a Creator
lessons.key_idea: Rubin argues that creativity isn't reserved for artists, because anyone who perceives the world and responds to it is already creating.

lessons.title: Tuning In to the Source
lessons.key_idea: Ideas are better received than invented, so the creator's job is to stay open and catch what is already flowing around them.

lessons.title: Awareness Is the Real Practice
lessons.key_idea: Training yourself to notice small details in daily life, without judging them, is the foundation of all creative work.

lessons.title: Collect Seeds Before Choosing One
lessons.key_idea: Early on, you should gather many rough ideas freely and avoid deciding too soon which ones deserve to grow.

lessons.title: Experiment Now, Craft Later
lessons.key_idea: Play and exploration come before refinement, and mixing the two phases too early smothers ideas that might have flourished.

lessons.title: Make It for Yourself First
lessons.key_idea: The best work comes from following your own sense of what feels right, not from guessing what an audience or market wants.

lessons.title: Finish, Release, and Begin Again
lessons.key_idea: No piece is ever perfect, so completing and letting go of the work keeps the creative cycle alive and makes room for what comes next.

plan.title: The Creative Act
plan.author: Rick Rubin (with Neil Strauss)
plan.confidence_note: I know the book's central ideas and structure well, but it is written as short, reflective passages with few concrete stories, so examples should stay close to its stated principles.
plan.one_liner: A legendary music producer argues that creativity isn't a talent you have. It's a way you live.
plan.summary: Rick Rubin, the producer behind records across hip-hop, rock and country, distils decades of work with artists into a book about creativity as a way of being. He argues that everyone is a creator, because simply living and perceiving is a creative act. Ideas, in his view, come from a larger Source, and the artist's job is to stay open and notice them rather than force them. He describes the creative process in phases, from gathering seeds, to playful experimentation, to careful crafting, to letting the work go. Along the way he urges readers to keep a beginner's mind, question inherited rules, serve the work instead of the audience, and treat self-doubt as part of the process. The result is a meditative guide to paying attention and making things that feel true.
